lesson_title: Collecting, Summarising and Comparing Data: Order, Count, Quarters
hook_text: Two schools. Same country. One box plot shows a 10-minute gap in every child's morning — and most people can't read it.
clip_script: Eleven learners from a rural school, lined up by how long they travel to school: 5 minutes at one end, a full hour at the other. No formulas — just count. The learner dead centre of the line? 25 minutes. That's the median, the typical morning. Cut the left half in the middle: 10 minutes — a quarter of the class gets to school that fast. Cut the right half: 40 minutes — and here's the sentence that wins exams — a QUARTER of these learners travel 40 minutes or more, every single day. Now the urban school, same country, same grade: typical journey 15 minutes, longest just 35. Put both box plots on one scale and inequality stops being a headline and becomes a picture — the rural box stretched wide, the urban box tight and short. One more secret: the average says 26,8, the median says 25. Why the gap? One learner with a mountain to cross drags the mean; the median doesn't move for anyone. That's why house prices and salaries always quote medians — the mean can be hijacked by a single millionaire. Order. Count. Quarters. That's data handling.
visual_style: Learners standing in a queue across the screen ordered by travel time, chalk lines cutting the queue into quarters; two box-and-whisker plots stacking onto one shared scale, the rural box stretching wide in red while the urban box stays compact; the mean sliding as one outlier walks in.
mood: Sharp-eyed and socially aware, the voice of someone who reads the numbers behind the news.
pacing: Steady counting through the queue, quickening into the two-school comparison, a pointed slow-down on the quarter-of-learners reveal and the mean-versus-median twist.
call_to_action: Watch the full lesson and read any graph the news throws at you.
